source_testimonies.care:
From a care-ethical standpoint, what matters first is concrete human need, the depth of vulnerability, and the reliability of our caring response—not the arithmetic of expected lives saved.

1. Moral attention to those involved  
   • The single trapped child is utterly dependent and powerless. If no one comes, the child certainly dies.  
   • The three adult climbers are in grave danger too, yet they possess more agency, experience, and mutual support. Their situation still allows a (partial) possibility of self-help, whereas the child has none.

2. Responsiveness and trust  
   Care is a promise: when we turn toward someone and say, “I will come for you,” we must honor that commitment. Choosing the one trip we know will succeed embodies steadfast, reliable care. Gambling with all four lives risks betraying everyone; a 60 % chance of leaving all to perish is a profound failure of responsiveness.

3. The limits of caring  
   As the corpus reminds us, “One cannot care for everyone; to try is to be overwhelmed and to lose the ethic of care itself.” Here our limit is one flight. Accepting that limit, we focus our energy where our care can be realized rather than dispersed in probabilistic hope.

4. Avoiding the rejection of care  
   To knowingly turn away from a child we can surely save would be to, in effect, “deliberately turn [our] back on the ethical.” That deliberate rejection approaches what the corpus calls an “evil [that] cannot be redeemed.”

Decision  
Send the drone to the trapped child. This choice honors the immediacy of the child’s vulnerability, keeps faith with the one life we can surely protect, and exemplifies the steadfast, concrete responsiveness at the heart of an ethic of care.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.deontological:
Maxim 1  
When I can certainly save one person but could instead attempt a risk-filled rescue of several others, I will forgo the certain rescue in order to gamble on saving the larger number.

Test  
All rational agents could not will this as universal law, because each individual would then be liable to have his or her sure rescue sacrificed for a statistical hope that benefits others. Treating a known person’s life as a means to a probabilistic aggregate good contradicts the requirement that every person be respected as an end in himself or herself.

Duty Involved: respect (and justice)  
Respect demands that no person’s life be used merely as a bargaining chip for uncertain gains. Justice requires equal regard for each person’s right not to be sacrificed.

Conclusion  
This maxim fails; it cannot be universalized without self-contradiction.

––––––––––––––––––––

Maxim 2  
When I can certainly save one person and no other sure rescue is possible, I will perform that certain rescue rather than attempt an uncertain rescue that might save more yet might save none.

Test  
All rational agents can will this as universal law: every person retains the assurance that, when his or her life can be saved with certainty, rescuers will not gamble it away. No one is treated merely as a means; each is accorded the full value owed to a rational being.

Duty Involved: respect  
By choosing the sure rescue, the rescuer affirms the inalienable worth of the person who can be saved, without reducing that person to a tool for hoped-for outcomes.

Conclusion  
This maxim passes; it can be willed universally.

––––––––––––––––––––

Deontological Answer  
Act on Maxim 2. Direct the drone to save the one trapped child with certainty.
source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Rawlsian Ethics Answer:

Behind the veil of ignorance we do not know whether we are the child, one of the three climbers, or even an on-looker. We therefore ask what rescue rule rational agents would choose if they wanted to secure the most defensible position for any person who might turn out to be the one in danger.

1. Equal Basic Right to Life  
   All four individuals possess the same fundamental claim to life and safety. “Each person possesses an inviolability founded on justice that even the welfare of society as a whole cannot override.” This forbids sacrificing a definite life for the sake of a statistical gain.

2. The Maximin Orientation  
   In the original position agents adopt the maximin rule: choose the option whose worst possible outcome is better than the worst possible outcome of alternatives.  
   • Option A (child): worst outcome = one person certainly survives.  
   • Option B (climbers): worst outcome = no one survives (60 % of the time).

   Because zero survivors is morally worse than one guaranteed survivor, maximin favors Option A.

3. Benefit to the Least Advantaged  
   The “least advantaged” here is whoever would otherwise be left to die. Option A guarantees that at least one currently least-advantaged person (the trapped child) is actually rescued. Option B risks leaving everyone in the same perilous state, which cannot be justified by the difference principle because it does not reliably improve anyone’s condition.

4. Rejection of Utilitarian Trade-offs  
   Although the expected number of lives saved is higher under Option B (1.2 vs. 1), Rawlsian justice rejects gambling with basic liberties or lives for aggregate gain. We must not imperil a certain rescue in pursuit of a probabilistic advantage that could leave all with nothing.

Conclusion  
A Rawlsian agent would send the drone to the trapped child, ensuring one definitive rescue and honoring the equal, inviolable right to life without exposing that right to the unacceptable risk of saving no one.
[/INST]

source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Step 1: List the concrete, stated consequences of each option  
Option A – fly to the child  
• 100 % probability the child survives → 1 life saved.  
• The three climbers certainly die.  

Option B – fly to the climbers  
• 40 % probability that all three climbers survive → 1.2 expected lives saved (0.4 × 3).  
• 60 % probability that no one is saved → 0 lives saved.  
• The child certainly dies (because the drone can make only one trip).  

No other outcomes are described; reputational, legal, or long-term incentive effects are not mentioned and therefore remain speculative.

Step 2: Compare the expected impacts  
Utilitarianism adds up well-being in expectation.  
• Option A: 1.0 expected life.  
• Option B: 1.2 expected lives—20 % more life saved on average.  

The corpus passage “When the numbers become extreme, our intuitions must yield” endorses choosing the higher aggregate good even when it involves risk or letting someone die. Here the quantitative advantage (1.2 vs 1.0) is clear and not merely hypothetical; it follows the same logic on a smaller scale.

Step 3: Identify missing information that could overturn the result  
• If the child’s remaining life-years or social impact were dramatically larger than that of the climbers, the balance could change, but no such facts are given.  
• If the 40 % figure were over-optimistic, dropping below 33 ⅓ %, Option A would dominate.  
Absent such contrary data, the stated probabilities govern.

Step 4: Rule-utilitarian considerations  
The decision is a one-off private choice; the scenario gives no reason to think it will establish a public precedent affecting future rescue behavior, so act-utilitarian calculus suffices.

Conclusion  
Because Option B yields the higher expected number of lives saved (1.2 vs 1.0) and no comparable downside is specified, utilitarianism recommends sending the drone to attempt to rescue the three climbers.

(If later information showed the success probability below one-third, or showed the single child had far greater expected well-being, the recommendation would reverse.)
